paragraphs: Scripture says (Deut 17:8): "If a matter is too hidden from thee in judgment, between blood and blood …".[{2}] He reports here that there are matters of aḥkām (rulings) and obligations that are hidden from the people and from the rest of the community, and that the imām al-akbar (the high priest, or chief authority) knows them. So: how does he come to know them? One of three ways, on Rabbanite assumptions: by naṣṣ, by naql, or by talqīn (oral instruction). It cannot be by naṣṣ (explicit text) — for then everyone would know them, since the text is available to all. It cannot be by ijmāʿ or naql — for these by their nature pertain to a community, not to an individual; even the word ijmāʿ (consensus) is etymologically a designation of a group. The only remaining possibility is istikhrāj and qiyās — derivation by analogical inference. There is no fourth option, and this is utterly plain.

A further consequence binds anyone who rejects qiyās and the probative force of reason in the farāʾiḍ. He must, on his own principles, forbid children and the deathly ill from drinking milk on the Day of Atonement — since Scripture obligates the fast generally and does not except anyone. We know the fast's not falling on children and on the deathly ill only by reason. Similarly: such a person must hold that the uncircumcised child is to be killed — since Scripture obligates death on whoever fails to undergo circumcision (Gen 17:14), and does not specify that the death-obligation falls on the guardian who failed to circumcise rather than on the child himself. The exemption of the child qua child, and the transfer of the obligation to the guardian, is known only by qiyās. And he would be obligated to punish children for every transgression they commit; to hold that the laws governing intentional vs negligent killing (Num 35) apply purely on their textual face without reference to mental state; and to obligate the ḥaṭāʾ-offering on every killer, even one who orders or writes from a distant city, or works by poison — since Scripture says (Num 31:19), "every one who has killed a soul," without exception. The discrimination by intent and act is known only by ʿaql and qiyās.

So too: Scripture says (Lev 15:10), "and whoever touches anything that is under him [the issuing-one] shall be unclean." Without qiyās, the donkey and the camel and the horse and other beasts that happen to be under the issuing-one are unclean too. (We know they are not — by qiyās.) Likewise: the betrothed maiden coerced is exempt from the death-penalty, by Scripture's specific provision; without qiyās, the unbetrothed coerced woman is not exempt. So too the boy coerced into sexual acts; the woman who coerces a man; the sleeping man (like Lot) violated unawares; and the man coerced into incest with his own mother, sister, or daughter — all require qiyās to extend the coerced exemption.

Likewise: when Scripture commands (e.g., Lev 11:25, etc.), "and he shall wash his clothes," the rejector of qiyās must wash every garment he owns — those in chests, in bundles, at the cleaner — since Scripture does not specify only the one he is currently wearing. We know it is only the one currently worn — by qiyās. Likewise: Scripture treats the ox and donkey (Exod 21:33–34, on the pit). Without qiyās, the same does not apply to horse and sheep. The prohibition "do not plough with ox and donkey together" (Deut 22:10) — without qiyās, one may plough with ox and horse. "If you see thy brother's ox or donkey going astray" (Exod 23:5; Deut 22:1) — without qiyās, if it is a camel or a bull one is not obligated. "Do not muzzle the ox while it threshes" (Deut 25:4) — without qiyās, muzzling other animals is fine. "Do not sow your vineyard with two kinds" (Deut 22:9) — without qiyās, sowing it with other plants that are not "two kinds" is fine.

The ox known to gore (Exod 21:29) — if its master is warned and does not restrain it, and the ox kills a person, the master is put to death. By qiyās, the same applies to any noxious animal — dog, etc. Without qiyās, only the ox falls under this rule. If the ox kills another ox, there is the rule of Exod 21:35 — by qiyās, the same applies to other animals; without qiyās, not. Scripture obligates anyone sleeping in an unclean house to wash his clothes (Lev 14:47), but does not mention the sitter. The sitter and sleeper are clearly subject to the same impurity-status; without qiyās, the sitter is exempt from washing.

Scripture (Deut 23:19): "Thou shalt not bring the wages of a harlot or the price of a dog into the house of the Lord." Without qiyās, the wages of a pimp are licit, and the price of a cat and a pig are licit. Lev 18:22: "Thou shalt not lie with mankind as with womankind" — without qiyās, woman lying with woman is licit. Scripture (Exod 21:26–27) obligates manumission for damage to the slave's eye or tooth. Without qiyās, damage to the slave's ear, nose, hand, or other organs does not require manumission.

These are some of the precepts that necessitate qiyās of necessity, and they have many parallels we have abstained from enumerating to avoid prolixity — but each will be discussed in its proper place in this book and elsewhere. If they claim that all these cases are known by naql and ijmāʿ — the very testimony of evidence falsifies them: the nāqila (the chain of transmitters) and the jamāʿa (the consensus-group) do not know these things and have not heard them. And if they retort that "these are in the Talmud and Mishnah," some of what we have mentioned is not in fact in those works; and what is there is not presented in those works as "we transmit this from the Prophet" but as derived "by naẓar" — and naẓar is the home of qiyās.

Know — may God set you right — that the appeal to naql and al-nāqila deployed by the muḥdathūn (the latter-day) of the Rabbanites is not an appeal known to the ancients of that school. None of the ancient Rabbanite disputants with our school denied qiyās; this naql-doctrine and the denial of qiyās is a new invention. It came about because the kalām-defeats of the ancient school pressed them, the absurdities multiplied against them, and they found no exit in naẓar — so they took refuge in naql, hoping to find there some room to maneuver. But by this they undermined the very foundations of their own school's positions, from which they took no profit. The proof that the ancient Rabbanites did not reject qiyās — that their statements are built on it — is what they themselves say at the head of their treatise on the Torat Kohanim (in the baraita of R. Ishmael):[{3}] "Of the thirteen canons by which the Torah is interpreted: qiyās al-manṭiqī [logical analogy = qal va-ḥomer]". Is this not an explicit declaration that knowledge of the Torah — that is, of the farāʾiḍ — is sought from these thirteen modes? The first of these modes is qiyās al-manṭiqī, which is found everywhere in their statements and on which they ground many things. Among these: that whoever touches the bed of the menstruant must bathe and wash his clothes; a fortiori, one who touches her directly is more obligated to do so.[{4}] Of such a fortiori reasonings their books are full. A second of the thirteen is kelal u-prat (the general and the specific): Lev 1:2, "If any man of you brings an offering to the Lord — from the cattle"; he reports that whoever wishes to offer must do so from something, and says "from the cattle" — the general. The plain reading would suggest one could offer any clean cattle. But Scripture then specifies: "from the herd and from the flock" — the specific. So only the herd and the flock are valid for offerings. Then the Rabbanites extended this by qiyās to: Lev 18:6, "No man shall approach any one near of his kin"; the general is "any near of kin"; Scripture then specifies twelve relations as forbidden — so by qiyās on the kelal u-prat structure, only these twelve relations are forbidden. Likewise for shaʿaṭnēz (Deut 22:11): the general principle ("no mixed cloth") and the specific ("wool and linen") yield: only wool-and-linen mixing is forbidden.[{5}] We will give full treatment of all thirteen canons in their place.

A further example of Rabbanite use of qiyās: from Lev 18:17 — "the nakedness of a woman and her daughter shalt thou not uncover, nor her son's daughter nor her daughter's daughter" — they hold that three generations downward (woman, daughter, granddaughter) are forbidden, since it is zimma (turpitude). They extend this upward by qiyās: woman, mother, mother's mother — three generations upward are forbidden. (Their qiyās draws on Lev 20:14: "and any man who takes a woman and her mother — zimma it is.") Since the downward direction has three generations, the upward must also have three. They have many such qiyās-arguments. They count the prohibited sexual relations at twenty: eleven by naṣṣ (text) and nine by naql (transmission) — the latter called firqāʿ or shniyot.[{6}] But they have also forbidden the brother's daughter, the wife's two grandmothers, and other relations that are neither in the naṣṣ eleven nor in their own list of nine. These three must therefore be forbidden by qiyās — there is no other route. The brother's daughter is forbidden by qiyās manṭiqī (a fortiori from one of the cases). The wife's two grandmothers are forbidden by qiyās jadalī (specifically by gezera shawa). This is the bone in their throats[{7}] — I mean, for al-Fayyūmī and his peers who would refute qiyās. They cannot extricate themselves from it except by permitting these three relations or by affirming qiyās. (As to their claim that these are firqāʿ, we will dismantle that.)

They also use a form of qiyās in the tractate Niziqin (Damages) — which is the fourth section of the six sections of the Mishnah.[{8}] On Scripture's saying (Deut 23:25), "When thou comest into thy neighbor's vineyard …" and (v. 26), "When thou comest into thy neighbor's standing grain …", they hold — by ʿaql and qiyās — that these two precepts refer only to the hired laborer working in the vineyard and grain-field, not to any passerby. For if the eating were licit to anyone, an entire caravan passing through could consume the produce, and that would be the man's destruction. So qiyās — applying reason to the situation — restricts the precept to the laborer. Likewise: they have obligated, in cases of doubtful impurity, the stricter path — so that no inadvertence may occur. This is obligated by ʿaql and qiyās. Likewise: in the case of a woman who has miscarried and the sex of the fetus is unknown, she observes 14 days of impurity (the longer one for a female) and 66 days (the longer one for a male) — by qiyās on the stricter. These are all openly available in their books, in numerous places.

Some of them attempt to refute qiyās by Deut 13:1: "All that I command you, observe to do; thou shalt not add to it, nor take from it." They say: if you have prohibited the brother's daughter and the sister's daughter — which Scripture did not prohibit — you have added. […] Reply: tell us about "do not add" — did He mean "do not add to what is written alone," or "do not add to what is written together with something else"? If "to what is written alone" — then why do you yourselves keep two days of festival when God ordained one? Why do you sit in the sukkah and eat unleavened bread for eight days when God ordained seven? Why have you forbidden the nine firqāʿ — the additional incest relations that are not in the text? Add this to the three we mentioned (the brother's daughter and the two grandmothers) — and you have added many things. If they say: "by 'do not add' He meant 'do not add to what is written and to what I instructed orally — that is, the oral Torah (the Mishnah)'" — then "do not add" means "do not add to what is written and something else, as you wish." Once the and-something-else is conceded, we can say: by "and something else" we mean what the writing itself obligates — namely, the qiyās that reason obligates from it. For reason is the measure of every thing, and by it truth is distinguished from falsehood, soundness from corruption. Our formulation is in fact more secure than theirs: we say "do not add to what is written and what the writing obligates"; they say "do not add to the writing and to something else" — which is more arbitrary. The objection therefore binds them more than it binds us.

A questioner may ask: what is the wisdom in God's leaving certain matters He wished obligated upon us un-stated explicitly (lam yanṣ ʿalayhā), making us return to qiyās in which there is contention? Wouldn't it have been easier — and avoided dispute — for God to articulate everything explicitly? And likewise: why did He place in His book defective and plene letters, equivocal names, ambiguous meanings? Would it not have been better to have all in plain, clarified form? Answer: since God (mighty and exublime) created intellects and made them the measure of all things, and entrusted to them the extraction of realities (istikhrāj al-ḥaqāʾiq) — and since the extraction of true meaning, and the distinction between it and false, occurs by the use of qiyās — God (mighty and exalted) wished to exercise our intellects, lest our path become like that of some non-rational animals which can be taught speech and merely repeat what they have heard (like the parrot and its kind). Were everything stated explicitly, there would be no difference between the wise and the un-wise; people would not be moved to seek wisdom. This is one aspect.

A second aspect: even if He had stated explicitly every commandment, prohibition, and license — given that He had also created the intellect with the standing we have described — we would still need to perform qiyās on what He stated, in order to understand it in particular circumstances. If we did not employ qiyās — the very use of which is constitutive of reason — we would have rejected reason and made it pointless; this dissolves the very foundation of religious knowledge. Moreover, in commanding us to use qiyās, He increases the legal-religious obligation and the opportunity for reward; for the more action there is, the more reward. As Solomon said (Prov 2:4–5): "And seek her as silver, and search her as hidden treasure; then shalt thou understand the fear of the Lord."[{9}] The first benefit of wisdom is the pleasure of it itself — Prov 2:10, "when wisdom enters thy heart, and knowledge is pleasant to thy soul" — and after that comes the reward of it; cf. Prov 8:19, "my fruit is better than gold, yea than fine gold; my revenue than choice silver"; Prov 3:14, "for her merchandise is better than the merchandise of silver, and her gain than fine gold"; through to Prov 8:35, "for whoso findeth me findeth life." We have given a long discussion of this question. The length is not wasted; the question is of great profit, since this matter is foundational to all the commandments: it is the bulwark on which most of what we hold depends, and the closing-off of a great fissure through which our opponents would attack us.

They have also asked: did not God (mighty and exalted) say to Moses on the mountain (Deut 5:28): "And as for thee, stand thou here by Me, that I may speak to thee all the commandments and the statutes and the judgments which thou shalt teach them" — He reports that He spoke to him all the commandments and statutes and judgments they would need, since He follows it with "to do them in the land"; and Moses then transmitted this to them as Deut 4:5: "Behold, I have taught you statutes and judgments, even as the Lord my God commanded me." If that is so, the qiyās-claimant's position falls — for qiyās has obligated us to forbid things God did not say, and Moses did not teach.

We reply: it cannot be the case that Moses taught all of the people all of these matters without remainder — for this is contrary to observation, and they themselves do not in fact claim this. Their actual claim is that Moses taught the general public (al-jumhūr wa-l-ʿawāmm) the public matters and reserved certain matters to be taught to an inner group (al-khāṣṣa). Now: what prevents their inner-group teaching from including the methodology of qiyās itself, with its modes and forms? In fact, this is exactly what we find: the use of qiyās is found in their books, current in their statements and disputations — in the Talmud, in Torat Kohanim, and elsewhere. We have already mentioned some of this, and what we have omitted is many times what we have mentioned. The plain meaning of the verse they cite, "I have taught you," is in fact a generic claim addressed to all of them, not restricted to one group.

This question in fact tells against them, not for them. If they hold that Moses had been instructed by speech and audition in all the uṣūl, furūʿ, and aḥkām that the people need, why is there the disagreement we have noted between the school of Shām and the school of ʿIrāq?[{10}] Why have the Palestinian and Babylonian Rabbanites split into divergent doctrines? This is the bone in the throat of every qiyās-rejector who claims that everything was known by naql and oral teaching — there is no escape from it except by sophistry. Moreover: Scripture says "and the judgments" (wa-l-aḥkām); but the aḥkām have no fixed boundary or terminus on which to settle — they extend indefinitely. Therefore it is necessary that istikhrāj and istinbāṭ (extraction and inference) operate on what arises, and that is qiyās, of necessity. In this lies the dissolution of the objection from its very root.

We further say: He said "Behold, I have taught you" in a generic form. If you find it licit to restrict this general statement to some specific group (the inner group), then we may find it licit to restrict the words "the commandments and the judgments" to some of the commandments and judgments — namely the ones that were given by oral instruction — and refer everything else to qiyās. The principle of selective restriction works both ways.

A further indication of these muḥdathūn-Rabbanites' departure from their own ancients (who never claimed exhaustive transmission): their teaching on menstrual and issue-blood. The Rabbanites themselves say that originally the discrimination between the kinds of blood was known only to the priest; and that — to avoid the doubt — the daughters of Israel later imposed on themselves a stricter rule: that if they see a stain the size of a mustard-seed they take seven days of purity, as a precautionary measure. They concede, in the very statement of this teaching, that the rule is not known in the absence of the priest, and that women have to abandon required prayer because of the doubt. Anyone who claims the rule is known by transmission has lied about the Rabbanites' own books.[{11}] ---
